library(jsonlite)

read_json_file <- function (arg0_path) {
  txt <- readLines(arg0_path, warn = FALSE, encoding = "UTF-8")
  fromJSON(paste(txt, collapse = "\n"), simplifyVector = FALSE)
}

mod_data <- read_json_file("western_amazon_basin.json5")

clean_text <- function (arg0_s) {
  s <- gsub("&", "and", as.character(arg0_s), fixed = TRUE)
  s <- gsub("_", " ", s, fixed = TRUE)
  s <- gsub("%", "\\\\%", s, fixed = TRUE)
  s <- gsub("#", "\\\\#", s, fixed = TRUE)
  trimws(s)
}

fmt_yr <- function (arg0_y) {
  y <- as.numeric(arg0_y)
  if (y < 0) return(paste0(abs(round(y)), "BC"))
  return(paste0(round(y), "AD"))
}

# Abstract

The Western Amazon Basin (4,31M km², encompassing 4.312.135 km² and 50.883 active 5-arcminute terrestrial cells) supported an extraordinary variety of sedentary, highly organised agrarian societies prior to European intrusion. Across six major hydrological divisions stretching from the Negro-Solimões confluence west to the eastern Andean foothills and south into the savanna wetlands of Moxos, pre-Columbian populations transformed fragile tropical soils and seasonally inundated floodplains into engineered cultural landscapes. Far from conforming to historic twentieth-century characterisations of Amazonia as a counterfeit paradise of ephemeral foraging hamlets constrained by infertile upland soils and scarce animal protein, regional communities engineered permanent anthrosols (Terra Preta do Índio), constructed extensive networks of raised agricultural platforms and causeways, excavated monumental geometric earthworks and built clustered proto-urban settlements.

Reconstructed across twenty-two benchmark horizons from 10000BC to 1542AD under PRETA, regional population expanded from 18,64k early Holocene foragers during initial colonisation to 135,9k in 5000BC as plant domestication of manioc, peach palm and native tubers took root in southwestern Amazonia. Growth quickened during the Formative era as ceramic technologies spread and intentional anthrosol accumulation created nutrient-rich agricultural substrata, lifting regional numbers to 620,3k by 1000BC and 964,5k at 0AD. Demographic acceleration accompanied the rise of monumental low-density urbanism in Llanos de Moxos, garden-city platform complexes in the Upano Valley and sprawling riverine towns along the Amazon trunk stream, reaching 1,88M in 800AD, 2,14M in 1000AD and attaining a pre-contact peak of 2,45M inhabitants by 1500AD (representing an aggregate regional density of 56,70 persons per 100 km²). Following early European exploratory probes along the Upper Amazon stem in 1541 to 1542, initial pandemic shocks and social disruption reduced regional population to 2,35M by 1542AD.

Demographic mass exhibited distinct geographic concentrations governed by fluvial hydrology and landscape engineering. The western lowlands along the Andean foreland supported the largest population aggregates: the Marañón, Huallaga and Ucayali Lowlands supported 540k inhabitants (74,45 persons per 100 km²), while the Solimões, Caquetá-Putumayo and Napo-Upano division sustained 520k persons (66,79 persons per 100 km²). Along the Central Amazon trunk stream and the Negro confluence, dense bluff settlements sustained 420k inhabitants (59,35 persons per 100 km²). In the seasonal savannas of southwestern Amazonia, the Llanos de Moxos (345,8k in 1500AD, down from its 1200AD peak of 380k) and the Purus, Juruá and Acre Geoglyph Belt (309,4k in 1500AD, down from 340k in 1200AD) maintained extensive hydraulic and geometric earthwork polities. The Lower and Middle Madeira-Guaporé sustained 310k inhabitants (65,47 persons per 100 km²), anchored by riverine dark-earth occupations and ancestral botanical domestication centres.

This demographic synthesis integrates 617 catalogued settlements with systematic geoarchaeological mapping of anthropogenic dark earths, airborne LiDAR surveys of monumental earthworks, palaeoecological core analyses and ethnohistorical chronicles. By subtracting nucleated settlement populations from regional rural baselines calibrated across 5-arcminute raster cells, PRETA establishes a quantitative demographic foundation for Western Amazonia. The results demonstrate that pre-Columbian lowland South America was home to populous, sophisticated polities that sustained high regional densities through sustainable agro-ecological and hydraulic engineering over millennia.

# Fluvial Ecology and Regional Sub-Divisions

## Hydrochemical Gradients and Carrying Capacity

The ecological architecture of the Western Amazon Basin is shaped by dramatic gradients in fluvial hydrology, sediment discharge and soil chemistry [@neves2003historical; @lombardo2022evidence]. Rising in the tectonically active Central and Northern Andes, white-water rivers such as the Marañón, Huallaga, Ucayali, Napo, Putumayo, Caquetá and Madeira transport massive volumes of mineral-rich suspended sediment derived from weathered Andean bedrock [@clement2015domestication; @lathrap1970upper]. These suspended silts are deposited annually across active floodplains (várzea), replenishing nitrogen, phosphorus and base cations, which permitted intensive, high-yield cultivation of annual root crops and sustained rich freshwater fisheries.

In sharp contrast, black-water rivers originating in ancient sandstone formations and lowland podzolic plains, notably the Rio Negro, carry minimal suspended sediment and high concentrations of dissolved organic fulvic and humic acids [@arroyokalin2010geoarchaeology]. These acidic, nutrient-deficient waters support lower aquatic biomass, driving human settlement toward high river bluffs overlooking floodplain confluences or encouraging intensive agroforestry and artificial soil amelioration [@macedo2017pedogenetic; @lins2015floristic]. Clear-water tributaries draining the Precambrian Brazilian and Guiana crystalline shields, such as the Guaporé and upper Madeira affluents, maintain moderate biological productivity and stable riverbanks suited for permanent sedentary settlement [@rocha2011regional; @watling2018direct].

These fluvial dynamics produced stark contrasts between narrow fertile riverine ribbons and vast infertile interfluvial terra firme forests. To overcome terra firme soil constraints, indigenous societies throughout Western Amazonia developed sophisticated soil management techniques, converting nutrient-poor oxisols and ultisols into fertile, carbon-rich anthrosols capable of supporting continuous, multi-generational agriculture [@glaser2004amazonian; @alho2018spatial; @golinska2014darkearths]. In seasonal savanna floodplains, where annual inundations alternated with severe dry seasons, communities constructed monumental canal and raised-field networks that turned environmental vulnerability into productive hydraulic agriculture [@erickson2000applied; @walker2004agricultural; @prumers2022casarabe].

## Six Hydrological Divisions

PRETA divides the Western Amazon Basin into six macro-regional hydrological divisions delineated by watershed divides, geological arches and river confluences (Table \ref{tab:subregions}):

### Central Amazon and Rio Negro-Branco

Encompassing the confluence of the Rio Negro and Rio Solimões at the Manaus tectonic gateway (707.720 km², 16,41% of basin area), this division includes the expansive black-water drainage of the Rio Negro and the lower reaches of the Rio Branco [@arroyokalin2010geoarchaeology; @neves2003historical]. Human occupation concentrated on high river bluffs around the confluence, where massive anthropogenic dark earth deposits at sites like Hatahara, Açutuba, Manacapuru and Osvaldo attest to dense, multi-tiered chiefdoms [@lima2002ceramica; @neves2014acutuba; @macedo2017pedogenetic]. By 1500AD, the division reached 420k inhabitants (59,35 persons per 100 km²), supported by intensive dark-earth multi-cropping, river turtle harvesting and regional trade.

### Lower and Middle Madeira-Guaporé

Covering the sprawling drainage of the Madeira River below the Guajará-Mirim rapids and its major clear-water tributaries, the Guaporé and Mamoré confluences (473.515 km², 10,98%), this division formed a primary early Holocene centre of plant domestication [@watling2018direct; @lombardo2020early]. Archaeological excavations at Teotônio demonstrate continuous occupation spanning nine millennia, with early cultivation of manioc, squash and peach palm followed by extensive dark-earth formation and ceramic manufacture [@watling2018direct; @porsani2017gpr]. Population expanded to 310k by 1500AD (65,47 persons per 100 km²), anchored by riverine trade networks connecting the Amazon main stem with the Bolivian uplands.

### Llanos de Moxos, Beni and Mamoré

Covering the vast seasonal wetland savannas of the southwestern Amazon in the department of Beni, Bolivia (937.523 km², 21,74%), Llanos de Moxos represents one of the most extensively engineered pre-Columbian landscapes on Earth [@erickson2006domesticated; @walker2004agricultural; @lombardo2020early]. Between 500AD and 1400AD, the Casarabe culture developed monumental low-density urbanism centred on stepped earthen pyramids, causeways, canals and thousands of hectares of raised agricultural fields [@prumers2022casarabe; @erickson2000applied]. Settlement peaked at 380k in 1200AD before restructuring toward dispersed fortified hamlets by 1500AD (345,8k inhabitants, 36,88 persons per 100 km²).

### Purus, Juruá and Acre Geoglyph Belt

Spanning the southwestern forested lowlands between the Purus and Juruá rivers, including the state of Acre, Brazil and adjacent northern Bolivia (689.397 km², 15,99%), this division is distinguished by hundreds of geometric earthworks (geoglyphs) carved into the clayey plateaus [@parssinen2009geoglyphs; @schaan2012sacred; @saunaluoma2018geometric]. Ditch-and-bank enclosures spanning circular, square and octagonal forms operated as ceremonial assembly grounds and nucleated settlements during the late Holocene [@carson2014environmental; @watling2017impact; @desouza2018earthbuilders]. Population peaked at 340k in 1200AD and stood at 309,4k by 1500AD (44,88 persons per 100 km²), sustained by palm agroforestry and terrace gardens [@peripato2023earthworks].

### Solimões, Caquetá-Putumayo and Napo-Upano

Extending across the upper northwestern Amazon from the Ecuadorian and Colombian Andean piedmont down the Solimões corridor to Tefé (778.619 km², 18,06%), this division supported dense riverine towns and highland-lowland interaction networks [@lathrap1970upper; @rostain2024upano]. In the upper Upano Valley of Ecuador, airborne LiDAR mapping revealed an urban landscape of monumental rectilinear earthen platforms and sunken agricultural roads active from 500BC to 600AD [@rostain2024upano]. Downstream along the Solimões, the Aparia and Omagua polities sustained nucleated riverbank settlements recorded by Carvajal. Regional population reached 520k by 1500AD (66,79 persons per 100 km²).

### Marañón, Huallaga and Ucayali Lowlands

Encompassing the immense Andean foreland lowlands of northeastern Peru where the Marañón and Ucayali unite to form the Amazon (725.361 km², 16,82%), this division supported the highest absolute pre-contact population in the basin [@lathrap1970upper; @myers1990sarabandero; @church2020kuelap]. Silt-rich white-water floodplains supported intensive maize and manioc farming, while the eastern Andean slopes housed fortified transit centres like Kuelap. Population reached 540k by 1500AD (74,45 persons per 100 km²), concentrated along active river meanders and lacustrine complexes.

## Fluvial Transport and Inter-Basin Exchange Networks

Fluvial navigation served as the primary circulatory system uniting Western Amazonian societies across vast geographic distances [@lathrap1970upper; @myers1990sarabandero]. The expansive river system enabled large dugout cedar and mahogany canoes, capable of carrying dozens of rowers and substantial cargo, to travel upstream and downstream along major trunks. High-value exchange commodities moved continuously between the Andean cordillera and the lowland forests: highland traders exported stone axe blanks, obsidian blades, salt cakes, copper ornaments and woven textiles in return for lowland feathers, jaguar pelts, curare poison, medicinal barks, wax and prized river turtles [@lathrap1970upper; @church2020kuelap].

Strategic confluences functioned as vital geopolitical gateways and trading ports [@neves2003historical]. The junction of the Rio Negro and Rio Solimões controlled passage between the upper Amazonian river systems and the northern Guiana Shield, while the confluence of the Marañón and Ucayali formed an expansive hub for ethnic confederations. Control over these aquatic corridors was fiercely contested, prompting late pre-Columbian polities to establish fortified bluff settlements equipped with defensive ditches and wooden palisades directly overlooking navigable channels [@neves2003historical; @schaan2012sacred].

## Paleoclimatic Shifts and Holocene Precipitation Fluctuations

Palaeoenvironmental records derived from lake sediment cores and speleothems indicate that Western Amazonia experienced substantial precipitation fluctuations throughout the Holocene [@carson2014environmental; @lombardo2020early]. During the mid-Holocene dry interval (6000BC to 3000BC), reduced monsoon intensity contracted evergreen rain forests and expanded savanna ecotones across southwestern Amazonia, particularly in the Llanos de Moxos and the upper Madeira [@carson2014environmental; @watling2017impact].

Human populations adapted to these shifts by intensifying landscape management. When wetter climatic conditions returned after 3000BC, expanding seasonal inundations necessitated the excavation of drainage canals, artificial settlement mounds and raised planting beds to maintain crop production [@lombardo2020early; @walker2004agricultural]. Rather than being passive victims of environmental change, pre-Columbian societies actively buffered climate variability through water storage reservoirs, raised-field hydrology and diversified agroforestry systems [@erickson2006domesticated; @clement2015domestication].

# Anthropogenic Soils and Agronomic Intensification

## Pedological Properties of Terra Preta and Terra Mulata

A foundational breakthrough of Amazonian archaeology over recent decades is the demonstration that widespread pockets of extraordinarily fertile, dark-coloured soils in lowland South America are anthropogenic anthrosols created by long-term indigenous settlement activities rather than natural geological anomalies [@neves2003historical; @glaser2004amazonian; @lombardo2022evidence; @silva2021hypothesis]. Known locally as Terra Preta do Índio (Amazonian Dark Earth, ADE), these soils are characterised by deep, black-to-dark-brown epipedons (pretic horizons) enriched in black carbon (pyrogenic biochar), calcium, phosphorus, magnesium, zinc and nitrogen [@macedo2017pedogenetic; @vasconcelos2019chemical].

Pedogenetic investigations confirm that Terra Preta developed through the continuous deposition of domestic debris: cooking fire charcoal, ceramic sherds, fish and mammal bones, shells, botanical compost and human excreta over centuries of sedentary occupation [@arroyokalin2012anthrosols; @macedo2017pedogenetic; @lucheta2015fungal]. Surrounding these primary habitation middens, pre-Columbian farmers created broader halos of brown soils known as Terra Mulata, produced by intentional low-temperature smouldering of agricultural biomass, weed mulch and organic waste during clearing cycles [@neves2003historical; @glaser2004amazonian].

The key agronomic advantage of these anthrosols lies in their extraordinary cation exchange capacity and nutrient retention [@alho2018spatial; @golinska2014darkearths]. In typical tropical Ferralsols and Acrisols, intense rainfall leaches soluble mineral nutrients, causing severe phosphorus fixation and soil acidification that forces farmers into short fallow-rotation swidden cycles [@denevan2001cultivated]. By contrast, the pyrogenic carbon in Terra Preta resists microbial degradation for millennia, preserving stable chemical exchange complexes that maintain soil fertility under continuous cropping [@lombardo2022evidence; @lucheta2015fungal]. Modern agricultural trials indicate that Terra Preta horizons support crop yields three to four times higher than surrounding unamended soils without requiring fallow regeneration [@clement2015domestication; @lins2015floristic].

## Geoarchaeology and Anthrosol Stratigraphy

Geoarchaeological surveys along the Amazon trunk stream and its black-water and clear-water tributaries demonstrate that anthropogenic dark earths are not uniform blankets but stratified cultural deposits that reflect dynamic settlement histories [@arroyokalin2010geoarchaeology; @arroyokalin2012anthrosols]. At Açutuba, located on the lower Rio Negro thirty kilometres upstream from Manaus, excavation profiles expose anthrosol horizons up to two metres thick [@neves2014acutuba; @macedo2017pedogenetic]. Stratigraphic analyses reveal alternating micro-laminations of charcoal-rich lenses, dense accumulations of crushed pottery sherds and ash layers spanning from 300BC through 1400AD [@neves2014acutuba].

Micromorphological analyses of anthrosol thin sections show that pottery fragments within Terra Preta acted as artificial micro-reservoirs, absorbing soil moisture and dissolved ionic nutrients while providing protective niches for beneficial mycorrhizal fungi and bacteria [@macedo2017pedogenetic; @lucheta2015fungal]. At the Hatahara site on the Solimões bluffs, radiocarbon dating of stratified charcoal series demonstrates that the accumulation rate of anthropogenic topsoil accelerated during periods of village nucleation, growing from initial ten-centimetre layers during the early Pocó phase to deep cumulative anthrosols during the subsequent Manacapuru and Guarita occupations [@lima2002ceramica; @neves2003historical].

## Biochar Stability, Pyrogenic Carbon and Nutrient Stocks

The long-term chemical resilience of Amazonian anthrosols stems from the molecular structure of pyrogenic carbon generated by smouldering fires [@glaser2004amazonian; @vasconcelos2019chemical]. Spectroscopic investigations reveal that Terra Preta biochar consists of highly condensed polycyclic aromatic rings with carboxyl and phenolic functional groups on their outer surfaces [@alho2018spatial; @macedo2017pedogenetic]. This macromolecular structure resists enzymatic cleavage by soil microbes while providing negative surface charges that bind calcium, magnesium and potassium cations, preventing them from leaching away under equatorial rains.

Nutrient stock quantifications confirm that total organic carbon stocks in Terra Preta deposits are double or triple those found in neighbouring native oxisols, with available phosphorus levels elevated by an order of magnitude [@alho2018spatial; @vasconcelos2019chemical]. Because available phosphorus is typically the primary limiting factor for agricultural productivity in tropical rain forests, the accumulation of bone-derived biogenic apatite and charcoal-bound phosphates transformed marginal bluffs into fertile agricultural oases capable of supporting permanent sedentary communities over many centuries [@macedo2017pedogenetic; @lombardo2022evidence].

## Microbial Ecology and Anthrosol Soil Communities

Soil biological profiling indicates that Terra Preta anthrosols sustain distinct microbial and fungal communities that differ substantially from surrounding tropical forest soils [@lucheta2015fungal]. Molecular sequencing of microbial ribosomal DNA demonstrates elevated richness of actinobacteria, acidobacteria and mycorrhizal fungi adapted to charcoal-rich micro-habitats [@lucheta2015fungal]. These symbiotic organisms enhance organic matter humification, facilitate nitrogen fixation and accelerate phosphorus solubilisation for plant roots.

The persistence of these specialized microbial consortia centuries after settlement abandonment explains why abandoned pre-Columbian anthrosol sites retain enhanced biological fertility today [@lucheta2015fungal; @lins2015floristic]. Rather than degenerating back into nutrient-poor forest soils, Terra Preta horizons maintain an active biological equilibrium that continues to fix atmospheric carbon and cycle soil nutrients, providing an empirical model for regenerative tropical agronomy [@glaser2004amazonian; @clement2015domestication].

## Ethnobotany of Manioc and Tubers in Southwestern Amazonia

The carbohydrate baseline of Western Amazonian populations was founded on the early domestication of root and tuber crops in southwestern Amazonian forest clearings [@lombardo2020early; @watling2018direct]. Manioc (*Manihot esculenta*) was domesticated from wild populations of *Manihot flabellifolia* along the transition zone between the Madeira and Guaporé basins [@lombardo2020early; @clement2015domestication]. Indigenous farmers selected both sweet varieties for immediate consumption and bitter varieties rich in toxic cyanogenic glucosides for long-term storage [@denevan2001cultivated].

Processing bitter manioc required sophisticated processing technologies: peeling, grating, soaking and expressing poisonous hydrocyanic acid using woven tipití basketry presses before toasting the pulp on large ceramic griddles into durable farinha flour [@lathrap1970upper; @lima2002ceramica]. Complementing manioc, pre-Columbian farmers domesticated arrowroot (*Maranta arundinacea*), llerén (*Calathea allouia*), sweet potatoes (*Ipomoea batatas*) and native yams (*Dioscorea trifida*), creating a polycultural root-crop complex that minimized the risk of widespread harvest failure [@lombardo2020early; @clement2015domestication].

## Ceramic Technology: Ceramic Tempering and Shell Middens

The physical production of durable ceramic cooking vessels, manioc griddles and burial urns in Western Amazonia required ingenious material adaptations to overcome fragile river clays [@lima2002ceramica; @neves2014acutuba]. To prevent catastrophic cracking during open-air firing and subsequent thermal shock during food boiling, Amazonian potters incorporated specialised organic and mineral tempers into the clay matrix [@neves2014acutuba].

In the Central Amazon, early Pocó-Açutuba potters utilised *cauixi*, the siliceous spicules of freshwater sponges (*Tubella reticulata*) collected from submerged tree roots in black-water igapó swamps [@lima2002ceramica]. In later horizons, potters adopted *cariapé*, the silica-rich ash of burned tree barks from the Chrysobalanaceae family (*Licania* and *Couepia* species) [@neves2003historical]. In the floodplains of the Ucayali and Marañón, crushed freshwater bivalve shells were added to clay pastes, producing durable tempered wares that withstood transport across regional canoe trade networks [@lathrap1970upper; @myers1990sarabandero].

## Agronomic Carrying Capacity and Yield Scaling

The development of anthropogenic anthrosols dramatically altered the demographic ceiling of Western Amazonia [@clement2015domestication; @neves2003historical]. Rather than being restricted to transient riverside campsites, pre-Columbian communities established permanent towns spanning dozens of hectares on bluffs above the Rio Negro, Madeira, Solimões and Purus [@arroyokalin2012anthrosols; @mcmichael2015phytolith]. In the Central Amazon around the Açutuba and Hatahara complexes, contiguous dark earth deposits cover more than twenty hectares with anthrosol depths exceeding two metres, indicating permanent habitation spanning more than a millennium [@lima2002ceramica; @neves2014acutuba].

By combining permanent multi-cropping of bitter and sweet manioc, maize, squash and sweet potatoes on Terra Preta soils with managed orchard fallows featuring peach palm (*Bactris gasipaes*), Brazil nut (*Bertholletia excelsa*), açaí (*Euterpe oleracea*) and ingá (*Inga edulis*), indigenous polities sustained sedentary population densities of 200 to 500 persons per km² on cultivated land [@clement2015domestication; @lins2015floristic; @watling2018direct]. These nucleated agrarian nodes served as economic engines for broader regional polities, supporting craft specialists, monumental earthwork labour drafts and defensive garrisons along strategic waterways [@neves2003historical; @schaan2012sacred].

## Agroforestry and Botanical Legacies

The carrying capacity of Western Amazonian populations was further expanded by sophisticated tree-crop management that blurred the boundary between wild forest and domesticated orchard [@clement2015domestication; @lins2015floristic]. Contemporary botanical surveys across the Western Amazon Basin indicate that hyperdominant tree species in modern Amazonian canopies are disproportionately those domesticated or semidomesticated by pre-Columbian societies [@clement2015domestication; @peripato2023earthworks]. In Central Amazonian homegardens and archaeological bluffs, indigenous palm species including pupunha (peach palm), tucumã (*Astrocaryum aculeatum*) and buriti (*Mauritia flexuosa*) persist as living legacies of ancient cultivation [@lins2015floristic; @watling2018direct].

Peach palm provided an exceptionally dense starch and lipid yield, generating up to twenty tonnes of fruit per hectare annually on fertile soils, an output rivalled only by irrigated maize or lowland tubers [@clement2015domestication]. Brazil nut stands (*castanhais*) documented throughout the Madeira-Guaporé and Purus basins represent managed anthropogenic orchards established along ancient trade trails and bluff settlements [@watling2018direct; @peripato2023earthworks]. These long-lived tree crops provided crucial dietary buffering against riverine flood losses, ensuring sustained nutritional security across seasonal hydrological fluctuations.

# Monumental Earthworks, Urbanism and Hydraulic Landscapes

## Casarabe Monumental Urbanism in Llanos de Moxos

The application of airborne light detection and ranging (LiDAR) technology has transformed archaeological understanding of pre-Columbian sociopolitical complexity in southwestern Amazonia [@prumers2022casarabe; @peripato2023earthworks]. In the forested savanna mosaic of Llanos de Moxos, Bolivia, airborne LiDAR documented an expansive, multi-tiered settlement system built by the Casarabe culture between 500AD and 1400AD [@prumers2022casarabe]. The settlement network comprises twenty-six documented archaeological sites exhibiting four distinct hierarchical tiers.

At the apex of this urban hierarchy stood primary regional centres like Cotoca and Landívar [@prumers2022casarabe]. Cotoca was enclosed by concentric double-ditch and rampart defensive fortifications enclosing 147 hectares, centred on monumental architectural platforms rising five metres above the surrounding savanna, topped by conical stepped pyramids reaching twenty-one metres in height [@prumers2022casarabe]. Secondary centres such as Loma Salvatierra (3,1k peak) and Loma Mendoza exhibited smaller stepped mounds and formal ceremonial plazas, connected to primary centres by straight raised causeways (*terraplenes*) and navigable canals extending up to ten kilometres across the seasonally inundated plain [@walker2004agricultural; @walker2011social].

These monumental centres were not merely ceremonial vacant shrines; they were low-density agro-urban complexes supporting substantial resident populations [@prumers2022casarabe; @erickson2006domesticated]. Cotoca supported an estimated peak population of 8,4k inhabitants during its floruit around 1000AD, while Landívar concentrated 5,1k residents. The Casarabe urban network integrated residential mounds with reservoirs, raised planting fields and causeways that doubled as hydrological dikes during the rainy season, demonstrating a degree of architectural investment and spatial planning on par with complex societies in the pre-Columbian Andes and Mesoamerica [@prumers2022casarabe; @erickson2000applied].

## Garden-City Urbanism of the Upano Valley

In the eastern Andean foothills of Ecuador along the upper Upano River, LiDAR survey and stratigraphic excavation have brought to light the oldest and most extensive urban agrarian network in the Amazon basin [@rostain2024upano]. Beginning around 500BC and flourishing until 600AD, the Kilamope and Upano cultures constructed thousands of monumental rectangular earthen platforms arranged in formal spatial complexes known as *plataformas* [@rostain2024upano]. More than 6.000 anthropic platforms measuring up to twenty metres in length and four metres in height were catalogued across three hundred square kilometres, clustering into fifteen major urban centres led by Sangay and Kilamope [@rostain2024upano].

Sangay concentrated dozens of platform complexes linked by broad sunken streets (*caminos hundidos*) excavated up to three metres into the volcanic clay, accommodating thousands of sedentary agrarian inhabitants (9,5k peak at 0AD to 400AD) [@rostain2024upano]. Kilamope (6,5k peak) and secondary centres were integrated into a continuous agricultural landscape characterised by rectangular drained field plots, irrigation ditches and defensive perimeter ditches [@rostain2024upano]. This garden-city urbanism combined high-density domestic architecture with intensive maize and manioc horticulture, erasing traditional boundaries between urban core and agricultural hinterland millennia before the Inca expansion into the eastern valleys [@rostain2024upano; @lathrap1970upper].

## Acre Geometric Enclosures and Southern Ecotone Earthworks

In the southwestern Amazonian rainforests of Acre, southern Amazonas and northern Rondônia, intensive deforestation for cattle pasture revealed hundreds of massive geometric earthwork enclosures (geoglyphs) carved into tertiary clay plateaus [@parssinen2009geoglyphs; @schaan2012sacred; @saunaluoma2018geometric; @carson2014environmental]. These enclosures feature deeply incised circular, rectangular, hexagonal and octagonal ditches typically measuring one to four metres deep and ten to thirty metres wide, enclosing central plazas spanning up to twenty hectares [@parssinen2009geoglyphs; @watling2017impact].

Palaeoecological cores and phytolith profiles confirm that geoglyph builders cleared small forest openings for earthwork construction between 2000BC and 1000AD while maintaining extensive palm agroforestry of *Bactris gasipaes* and *Astrocaryum* species in surrounding canopies [@carson2014environmental; @watling2017impact; @mcmichael2015phytolith]. Radiocarbon chronologies indicate that geoglyphs operated as corporate ritual assembly centres, defensive bastions and public gathering nodes for dispersed agricultural hamlets [@saunaluoma2018geometric; @desouza2018earthbuilders]. Recent predictive spatial modelling indicates that over ten thousand undiscovered earthworks remain buried beneath the modern Amazonian forest canopy, proving that southwestern Amazonia housed continuous networks of organised earthwork-building societies [@peripato2023earthworks; @desouza2018earthbuilders].

## The Purus and Juruá Riverine Polities

Extending northeast from the Acre geoglyph uplands, the alluvial corridors of the Purus and Juruá rivers supported extensive riverine chiefdoms that integrated floodplains with surrounding terra firme plateaus [@parssinen2009geoglyphs; @saunaluoma2018geometric]. Settlements along the lower and middle Purus were positioned on elevated river bluffs overlooking oxbow lakes and seasonal várzea channels [@lathrap1970upper].

Archaeological surveys in the middle Purus around Lábrea and Tapauá identify large circular villages enclosed by ditch-and-bank fortifications, affiliated with late pre-Columbian polychrome ceramic traditions [@parssinen2009geoglyphs]. These settlements controlled regional trade between the Acre earthwork networks and the Solimões-Amazon trunk stream, exchanging rubber, Brazil nuts and dried river fish for finished ceramic vessels and polished stone axes [@saunaluoma2018geometric; @neves2003historical].

## Defensive Architecture: Palisade Trenches and Ring Ditches

During the late pre-Columbian centuries, rising population densities along major river corridors led to increased competition over fertile anthrosols and strategic bluff locations, prompting substantial investment in defensive architecture [@neves2003historical; @schaan2012sacred]. In the Central Amazon at Açutuba and Hatahara, communities excavated massive defensive ditches measuring up to six metres wide and three metres deep across the landward approaches to bluff settlements [@neves2014acutuba; @macedo2017pedogenetic].

Posthole alignments along the interior rims of these ditches demonstrate the presence of substantial wooden palisades constructed of rot-resistant hardwood trunks [@neves2003historical]. Similar defensive earthworks, including concentric ring ditches and baffled gate entrances, have been documented across the southern Amazonian ecotone in Rondônia, northern Mato Grosso and eastern Bolivia, demonstrating that late pre-Columbian societies developed sophisticated military architecture to protect nucleated settlements and stored harvests [@desouza2018earthbuilders; @walker2011social].

## The Chachapoya Montane-Forest Frontier: Kuelap

Along the eastern slopes of the Peruvian Andes overlooking the Marañón and Utcubamba valleys, the Chachapoya culture constructed an extensive network of fortified stone citadels that anchored the montane-lowland frontier [@church2020kuelap]. Standing at an altitude of three thousand metres, the citadel of Kuelap (3,5k peak) is enclosed by massive limestone perimeter walls rising up to twenty metres in height and extending nearly six hundred metres in length [@church2020kuelap]. Within its ramparts, Kuelap housed more than four hundred circular stone dwellings decorated with geometric zigzag friezes, ceremonial towers and subterranean burial chambers [@church2020kuelap].

Kuelap operated as a political hub and fortified refuge controlling critical transit corridors between the Amazonian lowlands and the Andean highlands [@church2020kuelap; @lathrap1970upper]. Its strategic position enabled Chachapoya leaders to control the movement of lowland tropical products, including coca, feathers and medicinal plants, into highland redistribution spheres while resisting highland imperial incursions until the late fifteenth-century Inca campaigns [@church2020kuelap].

## The Solimões Várzea Chiefdoms: Omagua and Aparia

Along the broad white-water floodplains of the Solimões River, dense sedentary polities documented historically as the Omagua (Cambeba) and Aparia chiefdoms flourished during the late pre-Columbian era [@lathrap1970upper]. These riverine societies settled high natural levees (*restingas*) in linear villages extending continuously along river bends for multiple kilometres [@lathrap1970upper; @myers1990sarabandero].

Omagua subsistence combined intensive maize and manioc cultivation on freshly deposited river silt with organized aquatic harvesting [@lathrap1970upper; @denevan2001cultivated]. Large corrals built of timber stakes enclosed lagoons along river margins, keeping thousands of live freshwater turtles (*Podocnemis expansa*) for meat and eggs during high-water seasons [@lathrap1970upper]. Stratigraphic deposits at Tefé, Caiambé and São Paulo de Olivença demonstrate dense accumulations of Amazonian Polychrome ceramics, bone harpoon points and spindle whorls, reflecting complex craft specialization and inter-village trade [@lathrap1970upper; @neves2003historical].

## The Teotônio Archaeological Complex and Upper Madeira Horizons

Located at the principal cataract of the upper Madeira River near Porto Velho, Rondônia, the Teotônio archaeological site represents one of the longest continuous stratigraphic records of human occupation in South America [@watling2018direct; @porsani2017gpr]. Continuous occupation spanned from 9000BC through European contact, anchored by the rich fishing resources created by river rapids that forced migratory fish into shallow, catchable bottlenecks [@watling2018direct].

Archaeobotanical macroremains and phytolith profiles from Teotônio demonstrate that early Holocene foragers were managing manioc and peach palm prior to 6000BC [@watling2018direct]. By 3000BC, sedentary village occupation created deep dark earth middens containing some of the earliest ceramic sherds in southwestern Amazonia [@watling2018direct]. In later pre-Columbian horizons, Teotônio expanded into an extensive regional political centre (2,4k peak) characterized by dense anthrosol platforms, ground stone axe manufacturing workshops and large ceramic urn cemeteries [@watling2018direct; @porsani2017gpr].

## Hydraulic Aquaculture and Raised-Field Systems

Beyond monumental settlements and earthwork enclosures, indigenous populations in Western Amazonia transformed regional hydrology to engineer food-production infrastructure at landscape scales [@erickson2000applied; @walker2004agricultural; @lombardo2020early]. In the Baures region of northeastern Bolivia, pre-Columbian communities excavated thousands of linear zigzag earthworks across five hundred square kilometres of savanna, creating an artificial fishery [@erickson2000applied]. As seasonal floodwaters receded across the savannas, funnel-shaped earthworks directed retreating waters through narrow bottlenecks where woven basket weirs trapped millions of migrating fish [@erickson2000applied]. Captured fish were stored in artificially deepened rectangular ponds, providing a predictable protein source that insulated regional populations from seasonal subsistence shortfalls [@erickson2000applied; @erickson2006domesticated].

Concurrently, pre-Columbian farmers constructed raised agricultural fields (*camellones*) across hundreds of thousands of hectares in the Llanos de Moxos, the San Joaquín plains and the Guayaquil-Upano margins [@walker2004agricultural; @denevan2001cultivated; @lombardo2020early]. Raised fields elevated planting surfaces above the suffocating wet-season floodwaters while deep intervening canals conserved soil moisture, trapped organic silts and sheltered aquatic animals during the dry season [@walker2004agricultural; @erickson2006domesticated]. Agronomic calculations demonstrate that raised-field systems yielded carrying capacities capable of sustaining 150 to 300 persons per square kilometre of cultivated plain, providing the caloric surplus necessary to construct the monumental earthwork complexes of southwestern Amazonia [@walker2004agricultural; @denevan2001cultivated].

# Ceramic Traditions and Regional Horizons

## Pocó-Açutuba and the Early Ceramic Horizon

The earliest widespread ceramic tradition in the Central Amazon, the Pocó-Açutuba horizon, appeared along the lower Rio Negro and middle Solimões between 500BC and 300AD [@lima2002ceramica; @neves2014acutuba]. Pocó-Açutuba pottery is characterised by thin-walled bowls, finely incised geometric designs, red and white slipped motifs and modelled zoomorphic handles depicting frogs, turtles and predatory birds [@lima2002ceramica; @neves2014acutuba].

Settlements associated with this horizon, such as Açutuba and Osvaldo, occupied circular or semi-circular layouts enclosing central plazas, often defended by broad perimeter ditches excavated into bluff edges [@neves2014acutuba]. Ceramic discard patterns indicate that large cooking vessels and griddles for bitter manioc processing were in common use, marking the consolidation of sedentary village horticulture and the emergence of regional corporate identities [@lima2002ceramica; @neves2003historical].

## Manacapuru and Paredão Traditions

Between 400AD and 900AD, the Central Amazonian ceramic record underwent marked diversification, reflected in the Manacapuru and Paredão traditions [@neves2003historical; @macedo2017pedogenetic]. The Manacapuru tradition introduced thick-walled globular vessels with brushed surfaces and carinated rims, reflecting expanded storage capacity for fermented manioc beer and harvested crops [@neves2003historical].

The succeeding Paredão phase saw the development of nucleated bluff villages surrounded by complex defensive earthworks, including multi-tiered palisade trenches [@neves2003historical; @macedo2017pedogenetic]. Excavations at the Hatahara and Dona Stella sites show that Paredão communities expanded anthrosol accumulation through systematic domestic waste burning, generating deep Terra Preta profiles that supported dense village populations [@macedo2017pedogenetic; @neves2003historical].

## The Amazonian Polychrome Tradition and Guarita Phase

From 900AD until European arrival, the Guarita phase of the Amazonian Polychrome Tradition expanded along thousands of kilometres of the Solimões, Amazon and lower Negro [@neves2003historical; @lathrap1970upper]. Guarita ceramics are recognised by distinctive red-and-black painted geometric designs on white slipped backgrounds, anthropomorphic funerary urns with modelled facial features and broad-rimmed serving platters used in competitive elite feasting [@neves2003historical; @lima2002ceramica].

The regional expansion of Guarita pottery coincided with major sociopolitical centralization [@neves2003historical; @clement2015domestication]. Stratified bluff towns grew into sprawling regional capitals like Manaus and Manacapuru, where elite residential mounds overlooked extensive domestic quarters [@neves2003historical]. Funerary customs transitioned to primary and secondary urn burial within formal cemeteries, reflecting institutionalised ancestral veneration and hereditary status differentiation in late pre-Columbian Amazonian polities [@neves2003historical; @porsani2017gpr].

# Methodological Framework and Spatial Calibration

## Raster Disaggregation and Environmental Covariates

To estimate population densities across the 4.312.135 km² expanse of the Western Amazon Basin without resorting to arbitrary continental multipliers, PRETA employs a multi-scalar spatial disaggregation framework calibrated at 5-arcminute raster resolution (approximately 9,2 km by 9,2 km at the equator). The model stratifies the landscape into 50.883 active terrestrial cells, calculating local environmental carrying capacities using five continuous spatial covariates:
1. Hydrological category: active white-water várzea floodplain, black-water corridor or clear-water basin.
2. Soil fertility index: mapped extent of anthropogenic dark earths, alluvial inceptisols or weathered oxisols.
3. Fluvial accessibility: distance to navigable trunk streams and major tributaries.
4. Elevation and topography: low-lying floodplain, terra firme bluff or dissected Andean piedmont.
5. Macro-climatic moisture: precipitation seasonality and length of the dry season.

## Settlement Subtraction and Rural Baselines

Demographic estimation reconciles micro-scale archaeological site inventories with macro-scale territorial carrying capacities through settlement subtraction. Where archaeological excavations establish nucleated settlement areas and house-mound counts, local site populations are deducted from the sub-regional population pool before background rural densities are distributed across surrounding raster cells.

This prevents artificial double-counting: urban and proto-urban centres like Sangay, Cotoca, Landívar, Manaus and Açutuba are accounted for as nucleated demographic concentrations, while the remaining population is allocated across agricultural hinterlands according to local soil suitability and river access. The resulting density surfaces capture both high-density riverine settlement ribbons and low-density interfluvial foraging zones.

## Demographic Uncertainty Envelopes

Given taphonomic biases in tropical preservation, PRETA defines explicit uncertainty bounds for each benchmark horizon. Lower bounds reflect minimum residential footprints derived strictly from excavated ceramic middens, hearth counts and conservative family sizes (four persons per domestic unit). Upper bounds reflect theoretical maximum carrying capacities under intensive raised-field farming, complete exploitation of anthrosol deposits and prolific river fisheries. Across the Western Amazon Basin, the central estimate of 2,45M in 1500AD sits within an empirical envelope spanning 2,05M to 2,85M inhabitants, providing a demographic range that withstands regional archaeological revision.

# Macro-Regional Demographic Trajectories: 10000BC to 1542AD

```{r tbl-trajectory, results='asis'}
benchmarks <- c("-10000", "-5000", "-1000", "0", "400", "800", "1000", "1200", "1400", "1500", "1542")
disp_years <- c("10000BC", "5000BC", "1000BC", "0AD", "400AD", "800AD", "1000AD", "1200AD", "1400AD", "1500AD", "1542AD")

traj_rows <- lapply(reg_keys, function (rk) {
  r_obj <- mod_data$regions[[rk]]
  short_name <- switch(
    rk,
    wamz_central_amazon_rio_negro = "Central Amazon & Negro",
    wamz_madeira_guapore = "Madeira-Guaporé",
    wamz_llanos_de_moxos = "Llanos de Moxos",
    wamz_purus_jurua_acre = "Purus-Juruá-Acre",
    wamz_caqueta_putumayo_napo = "Solimões-Napo-Upano",
    wamz_maranon_ucayali = "Marañón-Ucayali",
    clean_text(r_obj$name)
  )
  pops <- vapply(benchmarks, function (bk) {
    viscount_fmt_pop(as.numeric(r_obj$population[[bk]]))
  }, character(1))
  c(short_name, pops)
})

tot_pops <- vapply(benchmarks, function (bk) {
  viscount_fmt_pop(as.numeric(mod_data$summary$headline_population_by_benchmark[[bk]]))
}, character(1))

traj_mat <- do.call(rbind, traj_rows)
tot_row <- c("Western Amazon Total", tot_pops)
traj_mat <- rbind(traj_mat, tot_row)
traj_df <- as.data.frame(traj_mat, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

viscount_table(
  traj_df,
  "Benchmark population trajectory across the six hydrological divisions of the Western Amazon Basin (10000BC to 1542AD).",
  c("Hydrological Division", disp_years),
  list(label = "tab:trajectory", font_size = "scriptsize")
)
```

## Archaic Colonisation and Early Domestications: 10000BC to 2000BC

The initial peopling of Western Amazonia occurred during the terminal Pleistocene, as mobile hunting and gathering bands penetrated the Amazonian forest along major river corridors and through the Andean-Amazonian ecotone [@lombardo2020early; @watling2018direct]. At the Teotônio site on the upper Madeira River in Rondônia, stratified deposits reveal human occupation layers dating to 9000BC, containing flaked stone tools and macrobotanical remains of palms and wild seeds [@watling2018direct]. In the Llanos de Moxos, palaeoecological investigation of anthropogenic forest islands (*islas de bosque*) demonstrates that early Holocene foragers were cultivating manioc (*Manihot esculenta*), squash (*Cucurbita* sp.) and chili peppers by 8000BC to 6000BC, establishing southwestern Amazonia as one of the earliest independent cradles of plant domestication globally [@lombardo2020early].

Across this Archaic baseline, human population grew at modest foraging rates, rising from 18,64k in 10000BC to 43,02k in 8000BC and 135,9k by 5000BC (yielding an aggregate density of 3,15 persons per 100 km²). Foraging bands relied heavily on riverine fauna, river turtles and abundant palm groves, maintaining high mobility between seasonal camps. By 3000BC (272,5k inhabitants), initial pottery traditions appeared along the upper Madeira and lower Solimões, coinciding with more sedentary village encampments and the intentional formation of early anthrosol horizons [@watling2018direct; @neves2014acutuba].

## Formative Sedentism and Ceramic Horizons: 2000BC to 600AD

Between 2000BC and 600AD, the transition to sedentary agrarian village life accelerated throughout Western Amazonia [@neves2003historical; @lima2002ceramica; @rostain2024upano]. In the Central Amazon around Manaus, the Pocó and Açutuba ceramic traditions appeared between 500BC and 300AD, marked by finely crafted polychrome vessels, modelled zoomorphic figurines and large circular village layouts enclosed by perimeter ditches [@lima2002ceramica; @neves2014acutuba]. At the Açutuba site on the lower Rio Negro, permanent village habitation produced contiguous sheets of Terra Preta up to twenty hectares in extent, accompanied by deep refuse middens packed with freshwater faunal remains [@neves2014acutuba; @macedo2017pedogenetic].

Concurrently in the Ecuadorian Upano Valley, the Kilamope culture commenced construction of monumental rectangular earthen platforms and sunken road networks around 500BC, initiating an era of intensive garden-city urbanism that lasted over a millennium [@rostain2024upano]. In the Llanos de Moxos, early ceramic cultures constructed pre-Casarabe residential mounds and raised agricultural fields [@lombardo2020early; @walker2004agricultural]. Driven by systematic anthrosol management and intensive floodplain horticulture, regional population expanded from 407k in 2000BC to 620,3k in 1000BC, 964,5k at 0AD and reached 1,62M by 600AD (37,55 persons per 100 km²).

## Classic Florescence and Monumental Polities: 600AD to 1400AD

The period from 600AD to 1400AD marked the apex of monumental earthwork construction, urban nucleation and regional political integration across Western Amazonia [@prumers2022casarabe; @neves2003historical; @parssinen2009geoglyphs]. In the Llanos de Moxos, the Casarabe culture reached its peak between 800AD and 1200AD, constructing monumental stepped earthen pyramids, causeways and canal networks centred on urban capitals like Cotoca (8,4k peak) and Landívar (5,1k peak) [@prumers2022casarabe]. Moxos population climbed to 380k in 1200AD, supported by hundreds of thousands of hectares of raised fields and fish weirs [@walker2004agricultural; @erickson2000applied].

In the Central Amazon, the Guarita ceramic phase (affiliated with the Amazonian Polychrome Tradition) expanded rapidly after 900AD, associated with fortified bluff settlements enclosed by palisade trenches, dense nucleated populations and extensive Terra Preta soils at Manaus, Hatahara and Manacapuru [@neves2003historical; @macedo2017pedogenetic]. In the Acre-Purus basin, geometric geoglyph construction flourished, providing ceremonial and defensive focal points for dense farming populations [@parssinen2009geoglyphs; @schaan2012sacred; @watling2017impact]. Along the Andean eastern slope, monumental masonry fortresses like Kuelap (3,5k peak) integrated montane and lowland trade corridors [@church2020kuelap]. Across Western Amazonia, population surged from 1,88M in 800AD to 2,14M in 1000AD, 2,38M in 1200AD and 2,45M by 1400AD.

## Late Pre-Columbian Zenith and Contact Dislocation: 1400AD to 1542AD

By 1500AD, Western Amazonia reached its demographic zenith at 2,45M inhabitants (56,70 persons per 100 km²) [@clement2015domestication]. Dense riverine chiefdoms lined the Amazonian trunk stream and its major tributaries, forming contiguous settlement ribbons where neighbouring villages were separated by mere hundreds of metres [@lathrap1970upper; @myers1990sarabandero]. The Omagua and Aparia chiefdoms occupied hundreds of kilometres along the Solimões and Upper Amazon, maintaining large fleets of war canoes, fortified riverbank towns, manioc storage pits and corrals of captive freshwater turtles to sustain large standing populations [@lathrap1970upper].

This high-density riverine world was witnessed during the 1541 to 1542 exploratory expedition of Francisco de Orellana, recorded by Friar Gaspar de Carvajal [@lathrap1970upper]. Carvajal documented continuous riverine polities capable of fielding thousands of warriors, advanced craft specialization and monumental timber architecture. However, the very fluvial connectivity that sustained these polities rendered them vulnerable to European pathogens. Eurasian infectious diseases, travelling ahead of physical European colonization along indigenous trade routes from both the Atlantic and Andean frontiers, triggered catastrophic mortality [@denevan2001cultivated]. Between 1500AD and 1542AD, regional population contracted from 2,45M to 2,35M, initiating a multi-century demographic collapse that transformed engineered cultural landscapes into the apparent wilderness encountered by later colonial explorers.

# European Contact and the 1542AD Baseline

## The 1541-1542 Expedition of Francisco de Orellana

The earliest detailed European narrative of the Amazonian trunk stream derives from the journal of Friar Gaspar de Carvajal, who accompanied Francisco de Orellana on his descent from the Napo River to the Atlantic between December 1541 and August 1542 [@lathrap1970upper]. Carvajal described sailing past continuous riverfront settlements where towns extended along natural levees for leagues without interruption. In the territory of the Aparia chiefdom, the Spanish were provisioned with massive quantities of smoked fish, manioc bread, maize, roasted fowl and live river turtles kept in fenced riverbank corrals [@lathrap1970upper].

Further downstream in Omagua territory, Carvajal described large multi-family timber houses, defensive palisade walls studded with viewing platforms and fleets of war canoes carrying hundreds of armed warriors equipped with shields, darts and throwing boards [@lathrap1970upper]. Carvajal noted that interior roads led inland from river ports into densely populated agricultural territories, confirming that riverbank settlements were integrated with extensive hinterland farming populations [@lathrap1970upper; @clement2015domestication].

## Protohistoric Disease Vectors and Depopulation

Although direct European conquest of Western Amazonia did not begin in earnest until seventeenth-century missionary penetration, demographic collapse preceded physical colonial occupation by decades [@denevan2001cultivated]. Eurasian pathogens including smallpox, measles, influenza and respiratory ailments moved swiftly along pre-existing indigenous exchange networks [@denevan2001cultivated]. Following the introduction of smallpox to the Caribbean in 1518 and the Andean coast in the 1520s, pandemic waves travelled down the eastern Andean valleys into the Upper Amazon trunk stream [@denevan2001cultivated; @lathrap1970upper].

Because Amazonian societies relied on dense riverfront nucleations and regular canoe communication, contagions spread unchecked through riverine populations. Initial epidemics caused estimated mortality rates of twenty to fifty percent among immunologically naive communities, disrupting social hierarchies, depleting agricultural labour drafts and causing widespread abandonment of defensive earthworks and raised-field systems [@denevan2001cultivated; @erickson2006domesticated].

## Post-Collapse Forest Regrowth and Taphonomic Erasure

The rapid depopulation of Western Amazonia following European contact initiated massive ecological succession [@clement2015domestication; @peripato2023earthworks]. Abandoned raised fields in Llanos de Moxos were reclaimed by savanna grasses and seasonal flood silts, while canals and fish weirs filled with alluvium [@erickson2000applied; @walker2004agricultural]. In the forested lowlands of Acre, the Upper Amazon and the Central Amazon bluffs, abandoned platform mounds, sunken roads and geometric enclosures were swiftly overgrown by fast-growing pioneer trees (*Cecropia*, *Ochroma*) followed by secondary tropical rain forest canopy [@rostain2024upano; @watling2017impact].

Perishable domestic architecture constructed from timber poles, woven reed mats and palm thatch decayed completely within decades under humid equatorial conditions, leaving only subterranean postholes, charcoal lenses and ceramic refuse middens [@neves2003historical]. When Spanish and Portuguese missionaries returned to the Western Amazon in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, they encountered fragmented, traumatised remnant populations residing in an apparently virgin forest wilderness, creating the persistent historical myth that lowland Amazonia had always been an unpopulated, untamed jungle [@denevan2001cultivated; @clement2015domestication].

# Settlement Systems and Gazetteer Synthesis

The PRETA settlement gazetteer catalogues 617 pre-Columbian settlements across the Western Amazon Basin, providing the empirical foundation for regional demographic reconstruction. Settlement peak populations range from early Holocene rock shelters and shell encampments (100 to 300 persons) to monumental urban centres like Sangay (9,5k peak), Cotoca (8,4k peak), Kilamope (6,5k peak), Landívar (5,1k peak) and Manaus (4,5k peak).

Settlement subtraction isolates nucleated urban centres from rural background densities, preventing double-counting and ensuring that aggregate regional populations accurately reflect the genuine spatial footprint of pre-Columbian habitation. In the Llanos de Moxos, settlement subtraction accounts for nucleated Casarabe capitals while distributing agrarian populations across surrounding raised-field belts. Similarly, in the Central Amazon, nucleated bluff towns are integrated with dispersed riverine hamlets. The geographic distribution of catalogued settlements confirms that late pre-Columbian Western Amazonia was an interconnected, highly nucleated landscape sustained by monumental landscape modification.

# Demographic Historiography and Continental Models

Historical demography of the Amazon basin has undergone profound revision over the past half-century [@denevan2001cultivated; @clement2015domestication]. Mid-twentieth-century environmental determinist models, exemplified by Julian Steward and Betty Meggers, argued that tropical rainforest soils imposed an immutable demographic ceiling of less than one person per square kilometre, restricting human societies to small, nomadic hunting and swidden farming hamlets [@denevan2001cultivated]. Under these minimalist paradigms, pre-contact Amazonian population was estimated at fewer than two million inhabitants for the entire lowland continent.

Subsequent revisionist scholarship by William Denevan, Donald Lathrap and Anna Roosevelt challenged these assumptions by highlighting the prolific resource base of white-water floodplains and the transformative potential of indigenous technology [@denevan2001cultivated; @lathrap1970upper]. Over the past two decades, empirical discoveries of anthropogenic dark earths, airborne LiDAR mapping of Casarabe and Upano urbanism, and extensive geometric earthworks have decisively dismantled environmental determinism [@prumers2022casarabe; @rostain2024upano; @lombardo2022evidence; @peripato2023earthworks].

## Epistemological Evolution: From Counterfeit Paradise to Domesticated Forest

For much of the late twentieth century, anthropological understanding of Amazonia was dominated by the concept of the counterfeit paradise, formulated by Betty Meggers in 1971 [@denevan2001cultivated]. Under this view, the lushness of tropical rain forests masked an intractable ecological poverty characterized by severely weathered soils, rampant parasite loads and low protein availability, which supposedly doomed indigenous societies to small, fragmented and nomadic groups incapable of state formation or architectural monumentality [@denevan2001cultivated].

This deterministic model has been replaced by the historical ecology paradigm championed by William Balée, Clark Erickson and Eduardo Neves [@erickson2006domesticated; @neves2003historical]. Rather than adapting passively to a pristine wilderness, indigenous Amazonian communities actively constructed their environments through long-term landscape domestication [@clement2015domestication]. By generating fertile anthrosols, modifying forest composition toward economic tree species, digging canals and constructing raised fields, pre-Columbian societies invested in enduring landesque capital that enhanced regional carrying capacity and supported dense sedentary populations [@erickson2006domesticated; @prumers2022casarabe].

## Comparative Demography of Lowland Amazonia and the Central Andes

A persistent legacy of twentieth-century Andean archaeology was the sharp dichotomy between highland "civilisation" and lowland "tribalism" [@denevan2001cultivated; @lathrap1970upper]. Lowland forest populations were conceptualised as cultural recipients borrowing ceramic and metallurgical innovations from sophisticated highland states. Recent research in the Western Amazon upends this unidirectional model, demonstrating that southwestern Amazonia was an independent centre of early Holocene plant domestication predating many highland crops [@lombardo2020early; @watling2018direct].

Furthermore, monumental urbanism in the Ecuadorian Upano Valley (500BC to 600AD) and Llanos de Moxos (500AD to 1400AD) developed architectural scales, road networks and hydraulic terraforming comparable to highland Andean polities [@rostain2024upano; @prumers2022casarabe]. The Western Amazon sustained 2,45M people in 1500AD at an aggregate density of 56,70 persons per 100 km², demonstrating that tropical lowlands supported demographic densities and sociopolitical structures as resilient and enduring as their montane neighbours.

The PRETA reconstruction establishes an empirical midpoint between uncritical hyper-populist assertions and obsolete minimalist estimates. By grounding demographic trajectories in 617 georeferenced settlements, pedological anthrosol extents and calibrated 5-arcminute raster cells, this synthesis demonstrates that the Western Amazon Basin sustained 2,45M inhabitants in 1500AD. This population was not distributed uniformly across virgin jungle, but was nucleated along fertile river floodplains, managed anthrosols and engineered savanna wetlands, representing one of the great achievements of pre-industrial human environmental adaptation.
